newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysia warns speculators, could use curbs.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysia warns speculators, could use curbs.

text.p: Malaysia's central Bank Negara on Wednesday warned of stern steps to curb speculation in the ringgit, but economists were divided over whether it would use capital controls.

Bank Negara Governor Ahmad Mohamed Don said in an interview with the national news agency Bernama that Malaysia would increase interest rates and hinted at possible capital controls to stamp out speculation in the ringgit, which has been under overseas selling pressure.
"Bank Negara will not hesitate to introduce measures to curb such speculative activities," Ahmad said.
The governor acknowledged that "while we are concerned about the impact of any such measures (to curb speculation), these... will not affect genuine portfolio and direct investors".

The economists said introducing capital controls would aid the ringgit by preventing its easy flow in and out of the country, but that would be against the central bank's avowed policy of liberalising the financial markets by the year 2000.
"Malaysia will be very cautious. If they are thinking of capital controls, they are setting the system back at least five years," said Jimmy Koh, economist at I.D.E.A. in Singapore.

He said Malaysia was also planning to launch a slew of new financial products by year-end, including a futures contract on the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange (KLSE) second board index, options on individual stocks and ringgit futures.
"If you are looking to launch all these products, then there cannot be capital controls," Koh said.
But other economists disagreed.

"Capital controls are nothing new to Bank Negara. They have done it before and I think if it comes to the crunch they will do it again," said Chiang Yao Chye, an economist at CIBC Wood Grundy in Singapore.
"He's (Ahmad) clearly talking about capital controls. They have publicly said they will not hesitate to use controls," said Dave Carbon, market strategist at Pacific Asset Management.
Ahmad said studies had shown that speculators have been the main sellers of the ringgit since the baht crisis began in May.
He said the massive and continuous buying of U.S. dollars in the spot and forward markets for non-trade related activities had contributed to destabilising the domestic financial markets.
"Such kind of disruptive activities has gone on for too long," he said.

Ahmad said the central bank had been in the process of normalising interest rates to levels that prevailed before its intervention in the foreign exchange market in May following a speculative attack on the Thai baht.
"Now we have no choice but to allow the rates to go up again," he added.
"They (interest rates) are up there," said Carbon at Pacific Asset Management, adding that "higher rates will be a nice silver lining for stability".
But, Andy Tan, regional economist at MMS International, said by stating its intent to raise interest rates, Malaysia could be allowing the speculators to make money in the forward market.
Interest rates in the forward or swaps market rose after the governor's announcement.

Dealers said Bank Negara intervened strongly in the market on Tuesday, spending an estimated $1.0 billion to help the ringgit end the day at 2.5060/70 against the greenback from 2.5247/52 at Monday's close. It touched 2.4950 on Wednesday morning, its lowest since May 20.
At 1000 GMT, the ringgit was at 2.5025/35 to the dollar against 2.5050 before Ahmad's interview hit the market.
Some dealers said the central bank warning was necessary as speculators were waiting to hit the ringgit.
In May, too, after a heavy attack on Southeast Asian currencies triggered by the Thai baht, Bank Negara had defended the ringgit by selling an estimated $1.0 billion.
Ahmad confirmed the intervention by Bank Negara to defend the ringgit, but declined to give the size of its dollar sales.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-201 4813)
